title: Research Methods in ELT

pts: Quantitative research measures and statistically analyses variables across larger samples, seeking generalisable patterns.
Qualitative research examines depth, context, and meaning through smaller-scale, often interview- or observation-based methods.
Both traditions contribute genuinely different, complementary kinds of insight to ELT research.

v: One research question on the board; two short, contrasting study summaries (written for this book)

items: Write one research question on the board, for example ‘Does daily extensive reading improve Class 8 learners’ English?’.
Half the groups design a quantitative study (what to measure, how to compare); half design a qualitative study (whom to interview or observe).
Groups present their designs in two minutes each.
Together, list what each design would reveal and what it would miss.
Discuss how a mixed-methods design might combine the two.
Use a question from participants’ own schools or from a current DIET research priority.
Support: provide a menu of methods to choose from.
Challenge: participants specify how each kind of data would be analysed.

blocks.x: Two designs for the same question (written for this book):

lines: Quantitative: four sections; two read graded readers daily, two do not; compare reading-test gains from June to March.
Qualitative: six learners keep reading diaries and are interviewed monthly about what they read and why.
A: The first tells us whether scores go up. The second tells us why some children keep reading and others stop.

body: Purpose: to show quantitative and qualitative research as complementary. Content: a pair of spectacles; through the left lens a bar chart, through the right a speech bubble and a diary page; the bridge labelled ‘mixed methods’. Style: clean line drawing. Board version: two circles joined by a short line, one containing a bar chart, the other a speech bubble.

items: Google Forms (free) for a short questionnaire in a quantitative design.
Taguette (free, open source) for simple coding of interview transcripts [VERIFY current version and hosting].

blocks.x: A two-column chart on paper: ‘What we measure’ and ‘What we try to understand’.

pts: True experiments randomly assign learners to conditions, isolating a specific variable's causal effect on outcomes.
Classroom research often uses quasi-experimental designs, given the practical impossibility of true random assignment in real schools.
Understanding this distinction helps evaluate how strongly a given study can actually support a causal claim.

v: Four short design descriptions on cards (written for this book)

items: Explain the key features of a true experiment: random assignment of individuals to conditions, a control or comparison group, and measurement before and after.
Explain that classroom studies usually use intact classes, which makes them quasi-experiments.
Give groups four design cards and ask them to classify each as true experiment, quasi-experiment or no comparison at all.
For each card, groups write one alternative explanation for the result that the design cannot rule out.
Discuss how confidently each design supports the claim ‘Technique X causes better learning’.
Participants redesign the weakest study to make it more convincing within realistic school constraints.
Support: give a checklist of three questions: random assignment? comparison group? pre-test?
Challenge: participants discuss the ethics of withholding a promising technique from a control group.

blocks.x: Four design cards (written for this book):

lines: Card A: 80 volunteers are randomly assigned by lottery to a vocabulary app or a paper word list; both groups are tested before and after. (True experiment.)
Card B: Section 9A uses peer feedback; 9B does not; both are tested before and after. (Quasi-experiment: the sections may already differ.)
Card C: A teacher introduces dictation and her class’s marks rise over the term. (No comparison: marks might have risen anyway.)
Card D: A school with smart classrooms is compared with one without. (Quasi-experiment with many confounding differences.)

body: Purpose: to show how design affects the strength of a causal claim. Content: a four-rung ladder from ‘one class, before and after’ through ‘two intact classes’ and ‘intact classes with pre-test’ to ‘random assignment’. Style: simple, clear. Board version: four steps drawn as a staircase with short labels.

items: OASIS summaries database (free) for one-page, plain-language summaries of published language research [VERIFY coverage].

blocks.x: Design cards written on slips of paper and sorted on the desk.

body: The labels ‘experimental’ and ‘quasi-experimental’ are about design, not quality. A carefully designed quasi-experiment with pre-tests, several classes and honest reporting may tell us more than a small, poorly reported true experiment (Mackey and Gass 2005).

pts: Case studies examine a single class, learner, or context in rich detail, offering depth at the cost of broad generalisability.
This connects directly to Unit 67's action-research approach — much valuable classroom research operates at exactly this scale.
Case-study findings are valuable for generating hypotheses, even when they can't establish universal claims alone.

v: A short case study (written for this book or from a teacher-research collection)

items: Read a short case study of one learner or one class.
In pairs, list what the case tells you that a large survey could not.
List what you cannot conclude from the case alone.
Turn one finding into a hypothesis that another teacher or a larger study could test.
Link the case to the action-research cycle of Unit 67.
Participants write a one-page case of a learner they know, with consent and a pseudonym.
Support: provide sentence frames (‘The case suggests… but we cannot say…’).
Challenge: participants compare two cases and identify what the differences suggest.

blocks.x: A case (written for this book): ‘Farhana, Class 7, a government school in Mysuru. Silent in English lessons for a term. After her teacher allowed her to plan answers in Urdu with a partner before speaking in English, she began to answer questions aloud. By March she volunteered in pair work.’

lines: Shows: a plausible sequence linking home-language planning (Unit 71) to willingness to speak.
Cannot show: that it would work for every quiet learner, or that planning alone caused it.
A hypothesis to test: ‘Two minutes of home-language planning before speaking tasks increases the number of learners who volunteer answers.’

blocks.x: Case studies are valued for depth, context and the generation of hypotheses (Duff 2008).

body: Purpose: to show the trade-off between depth and generalizability. Content: two wells, one deep and narrow labelled ‘case study’, one wide and shallow labelled ‘survey’. Style: warm illustration. Board version: a tall narrow rectangle beside a wide flat one.

items: Shodhganga (free, INFLIBNET) to find Indian theses that include case studies.

blocks.x: Photocopied case studies from DIET or cluster research reports.

pts: Meta-analyses statistically combine findings across many individual studies, offering stronger evidence than any single study alone.
Where this series has cited 'research shows' claims, they often rest on this kind of aggregated, cross-study evidence.
Understanding meta-analysis helps distinguish well-supported claims from those resting on a single, possibly unreplicated study.

v: The abstract of one meta-analysis; a simple ‘forest plot’ drawn on the board with invented values

items: Explain that a meta-analysis combines many studies’ results into an average effect size; a systematic review finds and appraises all relevant studies using explicit rules.
Draw a simplified forest plot: eight lines for eight imaginary studies, each with a dot and a range, and a diamond for the combined result.
Ask participants to notice which studies disagree with the overall picture.
Read the abstract of a real meta-analysis, such as Norris and Ortega (2000) on instruction or Lyster and Saito (2010) on oral corrective feedback.
Discuss: what does the combined result tell a teacher, and what does it hide?
Participants check whether a meta-analysis supports a claim from Unit 8 on corrective feedback.
Support: explain effect size simply as ‘how big the difference is, in a standard unit’.
Challenge: participants discuss how the choice of which studies to include can change the result.

lines: T: Most studies show a positive effect. Two cross zero. What does the diamond tell us?
S1: That on average the technique helps.
T: And what does it not tell us?
S2: Whether it helps in my class, with sixty children and no audio.

blocks.x: The combined result is stronger evidence than any single study, but it averages across contexts, and the studies included may come from settings very unlike yours.

body: Figure 81.4 From many dots to one diamond

Purpose: to explain the logic of a meta-analysis. Content: a simplified forest plot: eight lines with dots, a vertical zero line and a diamond at the bottom. Style: plain infographic. Board version: eight short horizontal lines with dots and a diamond below.

items: Google Scholar (free) and ERIC (free) to find meta-analyses and systematic reviews.
Zotero (free, open source) to organize references.

blocks.x: A hand-drawn forest plot on chart paper, kept for later sessions.

pts: Small sample sizes, lack of control groups, and researcher bias are common limitations worth checking for in any given study.
Publication bias — a tendency to publish positive, novel findings over null or replication results — affects the overall published evidence base.
This critical stance applies to this series' own citations too — genuine scholarly humility, not blind trust, is the right posture.

v: Three short study summaries with deliberate weaknesses (written for this book)

items: Introduce five common limitations: small sample, no comparison group, researcher bias, measures that do not match the claim, and publication bias.
Groups read three study summaries and underline evidence of each limitation.
Groups rate each study’s claim as ‘well supported’, ‘partly supported’ or ‘not supported’.
Discuss publication bias: what happens to the evidence base if null results go unpublished?
Apply the same scrutiny to one claim in this book.
Compare a newspaper report of a study with its original abstract.
Support: give a limitation checklist with one example of each.
Challenge: participants suggest the smallest change that would strengthen each study.

blocks.x: A study summary (written for this book): ‘A teacher-researcher trained her own class of 18 learners in mind-mapping for six weeks. Learners’ essays, which she marked herself, improved from an average of 11 to 14 out of 20. She concludes that mind-mapping improves writing.’

lines: Small sample: 18 learners in one class.
No comparison group: essays might have improved anyway after six weeks of writing.
Possible bias: the researcher designed the intervention and marked the essays herself, knowing which were pre- and post-test.

blocks.x: Publication bias, sometimes called the ‘file drawer problem’ (Rosenthal 1979), means that unpublished null results can make an effect look stronger than it is.

body: Purpose: to give a memorable checklist of limitations. Content: a brick wall labelled ‘Claim’ with five labelled cracks; a teacher with a magnifying glass. Style: light, humorous. Board version: a rectangle with five zigzag lines and labels.

items: IRIS Database (free) to see the actual tests and questionnaires used in published studies.

blocks.x: A printed limitations checklist pasted in the teaching journal.

pts: Replication — repeating a study to verify its findings — remains less common in ELT research than in some other fields.
This means some well-known findings rest on less replicated evidence than their frequent citation might suggest.
Awareness of this supports appropriately calibrated confidence in specific research claims.

v: Teachers or DIET faculty in a cluster
Two meetings of 60 minutes, a term apart
A short published or DIET study with a simple design

items: Explain replication: repeating a study, exactly or with deliberate changes, to see whether its findings hold.
Choose one simple published classroom study or a DIET action-research report.
Agree what to keep the same (procedure, measure) and what will differ (learners, school, languages).
Teachers in three or four schools carry out the study during the term.
Meet again to compare results with the original and with each other.
A conceptual replication: test the same idea with a different measure, for example a speaking task instead of a written test.
Support: start with a replication of a colleague’s action-research cycle rather than a published study.
Challenge: write up the replication for a DIET newsletter or conference (Unit 91).

lines: A: The original study was in an English-medium school in Pune. Ours are Kannada-medium.
B: That is a strength. If the result holds here, we know more; if it doesn’t, that is still a finding.

blocks.x: Marsden et al. (2018) and the contributors to Porte (2012) argue that replication should be treated as a normal, valued part of research rather than as unoriginal work.

body: Purpose: to show replication as testing a finding in new settings. Content: a recipe card labelled ‘original study’ with arrows to three kitchens in different places; two produce similar dishes, one a different dish. Style: warm, homely. Board version: one box with arrows to three boxes.

items: Google Sheets (free) for pooling results across schools.

blocks.x: A shared paper record book passed between schools at cluster meetings.

pts: Academic research aims for generalisable, publishable knowledge; practitioner research (Unit 67) aims primarily for local, actionable insight.
Both are legitimate and valuable, serving different purposes within the broader field.
This series has drawn on both traditions throughout, reflecting the two research communities' complementary contributions.

v: One academic article abstract and one teacher-research report (for example from Smith, Padwad and Bullock 2017)

items: Read an academic abstract and a teacher-research report on similar topics.
Compare their aims, audience, methods, scale and style of reporting.
List what each could learn from the other.
Plan one way to bring the two together locally, such as DIET faculty and a teacher co-planning an inquiry.
Invite a teacher-researcher to talk to trainees.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A comparison written for this book:

lines: Academic research: aims at knowledge that holds beyond one context; reviewed by other researchers; formal reporting conventions; often larger samples.
Practitioner research: aims at understanding and improving this class; judged by its usefulness to the teacher and colleagues; reported in accessible forms; usually small scale.

blocks.x: Borg (2010) reviews the potential of teacher research engagement and the conditions that support it. Allwright and Hanks (2009) describe exploratory practice, in which teachers and learners investigate puzzles about their own classroom life together.

body: Purpose: to show academic and practitioner research as contributing to one field. Content: two streams, from a university and a school, joining into a river labelled ‘ELT knowledge’. Style: gentle landscape. Board version: two lines joining into one, labelled.

items: ResearchGate (free) or institutional repositories for teacher-research reports and preprints.

blocks.x: A small DIET library shelf of printed teacher-research reports.

pts: Ask: what was actually measured, how large and representative was the sample, and does the claim match what the data can actually support?
This critical habit applies to published academic research, coursebook claims, and informal professional-development content alike.
This closes the loop on this series' repeated emphasis on evidence — genuine literacy means evaluating evidence, not just citing it.

v: Teacher education; B2–C1 for the learner variation
Trainee teachers, DIET faculty or senior learners
Five research claims from coursebooks, training handouts, websites and this book

items: Share a three-question checklist: What was actually measured? How large and representative was the sample? Does the claim match what the data can support?
Give groups five claims, each with a short note on its source.
Groups rate each claim on a three-point scale and write one sentence of justification.
Groups trace one claim to its original source.
End by rewriting one overstated claim into an honest, calibrated one.
With C1 learners, use claims from education news or social media about language learning (Unit 59 on critical language awareness).
Support: provide claims with source notes already attached.
Challenge: participants include effect size and replication status in their ratings.

lines: ‘Research shows that learners remember 90 per cent of what they teach others.’ Measured? Unclear; the figure circulates widely without a traceable empirical source. Rating: not supported.
‘Explicit instruction generally produces measurable gains.’ Source: Norris and Ortega (2000). Rating: well supported for the tests used; less certain for spontaneous use.
‘This app doubles your vocabulary in a month.’ Compared with what? Rating: not supported.
‘Several classroom studies suggest this technique can help, though most were small and short.’

dek: Unit 81 of 100: how the field actually knows what it knows — equipping critical, informed reading of research claims, including many made throughout this very series.

aims.x: This book has cited many studies, each time asking you to trust a chain of evidence you could not see. This unit makes that chain visible: how ELT research is done, what different designs can and cannot show, and how to read a research claim with informed, respectful scepticism, including the claims made in this book.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: distinguish quantitative and qualitative research and explain what each contributes;
explain the difference between a true experiment and a quasi-experiment, and judge how strongly each supports a causal claim;
recognize the value and the limits of case studies and small-scale classroom research;
explain what a meta-analysis or systematic review adds to single studies;
identify common methodological weaknesses, including small samples, missing comparison groups and publication bias;
explain why replication matters and why it is still relatively rare in ELT;
compare the aims of practitioner research and academic research;
apply a short critical-reading checklist to a research claim, a coursebook claim or a training handout.

why: Why this matters. This series has cited many studies and scholars. Understanding how that research is conducted supports genuinely critical, not just trusting, engagement with it.

background.x: Research in applied linguistics is often described as two broad traditions. Quantitative research counts and measures: it turns learning into scores, frequencies and correlations, and uses statistics to decide whether patterns are likely to be more than chance. Qualitative research interprets: it uses interviews, observation and diaries to understand how participants experience learning in context. Many studies now combine the two in mixed methods designs (Dörnyei 2007). Neither is superior; they answer different questions.

For teachers, the key distinction is between what a study shows and what it is later said to show. A careful study of thirty learners may be cited in a workshop handout as proof that a technique works everywhere. Research syntheses have repeatedly found that the quality of design and reporting in second language research is uneven (Plonsky 2013), and a systematic review of replication in the field found that replication studies make up only a very small share of published work (Marsden et al. 2018). These are not reasons to distrust research. They are reasons to read it well.

In India, DIETs have a research mandate, many teachers complete M.Ed dissertations, and the Shodhganga repository makes Indian doctoral theses freely available. NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 both envisage teachers as reflective professionals engaged in continuous professional development (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Teacher-research networks such as those documented by Smith, Padwad and Bullock (2017) show that teachers in low-resource classrooms can generate valuable knowledge of their own.

Most activities here are for teachers, trainee teachers and DIET faculty. Unit 67 introduced action research; this unit places it within the wider landscape of research methods, and Unit 91 turns to publishing research yourself.

items: Design critique. A one-page critique of a published classroom study, identifying its design, its main limitation and the strength of its causal claim.
Claim audit. A table rating five research claims from local training materials, with justifications and at least one calibrated rewrite.
Replication plan. A short plan for replicating one study in a new Karnataka or other Indian context, with what will stay the same and what will change.
Research pairing. A proposal linking one academic finding with one practitioner inquiry.
Which ‘research shows’ claims have most influenced your teaching? Do you know what the research actually was?
When did you last change your practice because of evidence? What kind of evidence was it?
How might publication bias affect the advice given in teacher-training workshops?
What would count as good evidence for a technique in your own classroom?
How do you respond when research conflicts with your own classroom experience?

Screenshots of Google Scholar, Google Forms, Taguette, Zotero, OASIS, IRIS or Shodhganga require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Abstracts quoted in training must be cited in full, and learner cases require consent and pseudonyms.

terms.def: An in-depth study of one person, class or institution in its real context, often using several kinds of data, such as observation, interviews and learners’ work.

A statistic showing how large a difference or relationship is, in a standard unit, rather than only whether it is statistically significant. Meta-analyses combine effect sizes from many studies into an average.

A statistical method that combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate an overall effect size; its conclusions depend on the quality of the studies included and on publication bias.

A research design that combines quantitative and qualitative data and analysis within one study, for example test scores together with learner interviews, so that each type of evidence helps to explain the other.
The tendency for studies with positive or significant results to be published more often than those with null results, which can distort the research picture.
Research that gathers and interprets non-numerical data, such as interviews, observations, diaries or classroom recordings, to understand experiences, perspectives and meanings in depth.
Research that gathers and analyses numerical data, such as test scores or survey responses, using statistics to measure variables, compare groups or test relationships between them.
An experimental study that compares groups that were not randomly assigned, such as two existing sections in a school; it is common in classroom research but weaker in ruling out other explanations.

Repeating a research study, exactly or with planned changes, to see whether its findings hold in another setting or with other participants. Replication is essential before a single study’s results are treated as reliable evidence for practice.

A research review that searches for, selects and appraises all relevant studies on a question using explicit, replicable methods, often combining results statistically. It gives stronger evidence than a single study.
